title: Tenant-visible misordering and slow responses — customer brief & recovery guide
content:
Summary for customers (short):

On 2029-10-28 02:12 UTC Redwood experienced a region-scoped degradation that caused a subset of requests in the EU region to return stale or misordered streaming tokens and increased tail latency for certain tenant workloads. The issue affected roughly 4% of requests routed through the EU serving cluster for a window of ~42 minutes. We routed traffic away from the impacted pool and applied a configuration rollback at 02:58 UTC. Service returned to normal by 03:07 UTC.

Impact (what customers saw):
- Some streaming responses had out-of-order token fragments making structured streaming outputs invalid for a minority of sessions.
- Affected customers also reported elevated 99th percentile latency for non-streaming generation calls (peak 1.8s vs baseline 320ms).
- No customer data was lost; request payloads and KV cache content were preserved.

High-level timeline (UTC):
- 02:12 — First anomalous traces alert: unusual KV cache miss pattern + reorder metric (SRE alerted).
- 02:15 — On-call SRE investigates; correlates with recent routing config change deployed to EU pool (rollout INF-9876).
- 02:22 — Engineering confirms partial cache stampede and an ordering regression in the streaming assembler microservice.
- 02:30 — We start gradual traffic draining from the affected instance group and enable more aggressive request timeouts to reduce head-of-line blocking.
- 02:58 — Decision to rollback routing config to previous stable 2029-10-27-3; rollback started.
- 03:07 — Telemetry shows latency and reorder metrics back to baseline; rollback complete.
- 03:30 — Post-incident validation and watch initiated.

Root cause (customer-facing explanation):
A recent routing configuration change meant to optimize placement for cold-starts unintentionally increased the number of concurrent requests sent to a small set of GPU serving instances. Under that load pattern, the streaming assembler service (which rehydrates token fragments and maintains ordering for streaming outputs) hit a race condition when KV cache hits and asynchronous fragment callbacks interleaved in an unexpected sequence. This produced misordered token fragments for a small portion of sessions and caused head-of-line blocking that raised tail latency for other requests routed to the same nodes.

Why this affected streaming more than sync generation:
Streaming relies on an ordering guarantee across asynchronous callbacks; a rare interleaving of cache hits and late-arriving fragments broke that assumption. Sync generation flows are less sensitive because they wait for a single assembled result before returning.

Immediate mitigations we applied:
- Rolled back the routing configuration to the prior revision (removes aggressive co-location optimization).
- Drained traffic from the small, impacted instance pool to prevent further cache contention.
- Applied a conservative per-tenant concurrency cap for EU region for 24 hours to reduce blast radius while we instrument deeper fixes.

Customer-visible actions and what you can do: (clear, actionable)
- No customer API key rotation or configuration changes required.
- If you noticed truncated or misordered streaming outputs, please re-run the request; tokens and model state were not lost — a fresh request will produce a full, ordered response.
- If your product has automated stream parsers, consider adding an idempotent reassembly step that validates sequence numbers and retries automatically on missing fragments for the next 48 hours.

Compensation and SLA considerations:
- We are tracking affected customers and API usage during the window to determine credit eligibility. Affected customers will be contacted directly by their account leads by 2029-11-01 with an impact summary and proposed credit.

Technical follow-up plan (what engineering is committing to):
- Short term (<= 7 days): add stricter ordering checks & guardrails in the streaming assembler, add a non-disruptive canary for routing config changes, and tune the auto-throttle thresholds for EU serving pools.
- Medium term (<= 30 days): refactor the assembler to process fragments under an explicit ordering queue that is resilient to late callbacks and add an end-to-end test that simulates the KV-hit/late-fragment interleaving.
- Longer term (<= 90 days): revisit routing placement heuristics and expose a per-tenant placement override to reduce co-location risk for high-concurrency tenants.

Status page wording (suggested):
Title: Brief regional degradation — EU streaming ordering + tail latency (resolved)\Summary: Between 02:12 UTC and 03:07 UTC on 2029-10-28 we observed a regional degradation affecting streaming ordering and tail latency for a subset of requests in our EU region. We rolled back a recent routing config change which resolved the issue. No customer data loss is expected. We will follow up individually with affected customers.

FAQ for customer success reps (quick answers):
Q: Was customer data exposed or lost?
A: No. Payloads and KV cache contents remain intact. The issue impacted ordering of streamed tokens only.

Q: Will this happen again?
A: We have mitigations in place and are delivering code fixes and improved testing. We will also add preflight canaries for routing changes.

Q: I still see a degraded session after 03:07 UTC — what now?
A: Please open a ticket referencing JIRA-INF-9876 and include request IDs (x-request-id). We will prioritize follow-up.

Internal notes / decision log (notes to self — rough):
- Consider adding a lightweight sequence-number checksum in the streaming wire protocol. Low friction, could reduce customer-visible misordering in the event of late fragments.
- Why did rollout target small pool? check rollout criteria and autogrouping logic (PR: github.com/redwood/infer/PR-4521).
- Follow-up with SRE on whether autoscaler behaved correctly — telemetry suggests some nodes were at 98% util. Might need a preemptive capacity buffer for EU.

Draft outreach cadence (for review):
1) Short status page post (now) + targeted emails to affected accounts (within 6 hours).
2) Follow-up with a technical summary and timeline (within 72 hours).
3) Individual remediation/credit discussion (by 2029-11-01).

Open questions for engineering (to resolve before final customer postmortem):
- Exact concurrency thresholds that created the race (TBD: INF-9876:analysis).
- Whether any tenants experienced repeated failures on subsequent requests (need request-level audit).
- Confirm that rollback fully removed co-location config across all EU AZs (cross-check with infra state).

Contact for customers:
- For urgent follow-up, please contact your account lead or customer-success@redwood.ai with subject: "INC-9876 follow-up". Include sample request IDs and the approximate timestamp.

Apology and close:
We apologize for the disruption. We recognize streaming correctness and predictable latency are essential to your product experience. Our engineering and SRE teams are treating this as high priority and we will share a more detailed, finalized postmortem once the follow-up analysis completes.

--- end of draft ---
